solutions.text: \(\frac{2}{\pi}\) The main idea lies on the fact that positive integers are uniformly distributed modulo \(\pi\). (In the other words, if each integer \(n\) is written as \(q \pi+r\) where \(q\) is an integer and \(0 \leq r<\pi\), the value of \(r\) will distribute uniformly in the interval \([0, \pi]\).) Using this fact, the summation is equivalent to the average value (using the Riemann summation) of the function \(|\cos (k)|\) over the interval \([0, \pi]\). Therefore, the answer is \(\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi}|\cos (k)|=\frac{2}{\pi}\).
